title: Every pane says what it is for, in words somebody already knows
goal: The panel's sections are named in words the app invented, so you have to open one to find out what it does and open it again next time because the name never told you. Somebody looking at a component sees Versions and Adjustable and can tell you what neither of them is for. Name every section for the job it does, using the words this kind of tool already uses, so the panel becomes predictable.
notes:
Said by the user on 2026-09-15 while looking at a component: "i don't even know what 'Versions' is", then "what the hell is adjustable? Component properties? How is 'adjustable' different from anything? This is completely messy IA and ux", and then the summary that should govern this task: "panes purposes should be predictable and clear. It is neither now."

TWO INVENTED NAMES WHERE STANDARD ONES EXIST, and the user guessed the right answer for one of them out loud.

1. 'Adjustable' is this app's word for the things a copy can be given its own values for. Every other tool calls those properties or parameters. The user's own guess, 'Component properties?', is almost certainly the answer, and the fact that they had to guess is the bug. The word also fails on its own terms: everything in the panel is adjustable, so it does not distinguish anything, which is exactly what they said.

2. 'Versions' is this app's word for what the rest of the industry calls variants. This is already recorded as a known divergence: the tutorial guide componentVersions carries a comment saying 'It is called Versions because that is what the panel calls it. The task that asked for this track said Variants, and a guide teaches what shipped rather than what the plan called it.' So the plan said variants, the panel said versions, and the tutorial had to follow the panel. Fix the panel and the rest lines up.

The deeper rule the user is asking for is predictability, so do not stop at two renames. Go through every section and ask whether its name answers 'what is this for'. Where a section needs a paragraph inside it to explain itself - and several do, Versions has three lines of prose under it in the screenshot - the paragraph is a symptom and the name is the disease.

This is the same complaint as the clutter tasks filed alongside it and should be read with them: position-and-size-leave-the-panel, one-row-for-a-number-that-has-four-sides, the-panel-shows-the-panes-that-matter-and-you-ca, and a-copy-of-a-component-is-configured-not-authored. A shorter panel full of unclear names is still unpredictable, and clear names on a wall of sections are still a wall.

Renaming is cheap to do and expensive to do halfway. The tutorials point at panel sections by name and there is a check that fails the build when a guide points at something that has gone, so a rename that misses a guide will be caught - but only if the guides are rebuilt, so run them.

THE MODEL, corrected by the user on 2026-09-15 while walking away. First: "I don't think 'Variants' is any better. component properties makes sense. Variant is a property of the component." Then, still thinking: "Maybe State is a separate property. or maybe variant is hierarchical."

So the direction is ONE concept, not two sections. A component has PROPERTIES. What the panel currently splits into 'Adjustable' and 'Versions' is one list: a property is anything a copy can be given its own answer for, and one KIND of property is a set of named looks, which is what Versions is today. That is why neither name worked: they are two names for halves of one idea.

This also collapses the copy's panel into the same list with values in it instead of definitions, which is what the sibling task a-copy-of-a-component-is-configured-not-authored is for.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN, and the user was explicitly unsure, so settle it with a prototype rather than a preference:
- Is a state just one property among many, named State with the values rest, hovered, pressed and disabled? That is the simplest answer and probably right.
- Or does a component need more than one look-changing property at once, so that a Button has a Type of primary or secondary AND a State of rest or hovered, and the two combine into a matrix of drawings? That is what the user means by variant being hierarchical, and it is what real button components need almost immediately.
The second is strictly more powerful and strictly more work, and the first is a special case of it. Prototype the matrix case before choosing, because designing for one look-changing property and discovering later that two are needed is a rewrite rather than an addition.

Do NOT settle this by picking a word. The question is whether the model holds one named-set property or several, and the naming falls out of the answer.
acceptance: Every section in the panel is named for what it is for, and the audit lists each name with the one sentence that justifies it
Versions and Adjustable in particular are renamed to what they actually are, using terms somebody who has used a design tool would recognise rather than terms this app coined
A section's name plus one short line is enough to know whether to open it, without opening it

The explanatory paragraphs currently sitting inside sections are cut back hard: a section that needs three lines of prose to explain itself is misnamed, and the audit says which ones were fixed by renaming rather than by rewording
The same names are used everywhere they appear: the panel, the menus, the tutorials and the tooltips do not use three words for one thing
Nothing is renamed without following it through: grep for the old word and fix the guides, walks and help text that used it, or the app teaches a word it no longer uses
A first-time check with somebody who has not seen it: they can say what each section is for from the name alone, and whatever they got wrong is written down
Audit under queue/audits/ with the panel before and after for a component original, a component copy and a plain shape, and anything rough filed as a follow-up

log.note: user corrected the direction: one Properties list, with a variant or state as a kind of property; open question whether several look-changing properties combine
